Can you summarize Jim Healy's career as a local broadcaster and his famous drive-time sports show? Answer according to: Our mission this morning, and we choose to accept it, is to tell you about a man that many of you never knew. Sadly.
Twelve years ago today, Jim Healy died. He was a local broadcaster who had an evening drive-time sports show. A form of it started in 1961 and it didn't end until May 1994, less than two months before he died. For most of his career, he was on KLAC, but he moved to KMPC for the last seven or eight years.
When he died of cancer, it surprised many because he hadn't been off the air long and had been quiet about his absence.
"He was from the old school, the Depression Era," said his son, Channel 4 news reporter Patrick Healy. "You don't say much, you show no signs of weakness or vulnerability."
His show, a freeway ritual for many, is hard to describe. It was a daily report of sports events, with an emphasis on the stupid and juicy. And it was sprinkled, sometimes dominated, by sound bites of various sports people. He had an entire library of them, and nothing made him happier than when somebody came to him with a fresh tape of a sports big shot, losing it.
That's what happened on May 14, 1978, when a young reporter named Paul Olden, now on KNX but then working for Healy, came to Healy with a tape of Tom Lasorda after a game in which Dave Kingman had destroyed the Dodgers. Olden asked Lasorda a simple question: "What's your opinion of Kingman's performance?"
But the fire had been lighted. Lasorda started at mild yell and quickly got to top decibels.
Fourteen bleeps later, Lasorda was done and Healy had hit the jackpot. He had taught young Olden to never turn off the tape recorder, no matter what. And his protege had delivered. Before long, Lasorda on Kingman became the standard by which all other tirades were measured.
Healy's sound bites remain alive and well. There are several websites still collecting them and spreading them around, and Richard Perelman, the press chief for the 1984 Olympics, has done several pilot shows in the Healy model that he is trying to sell to California stations, most of them managed by people who never knew and don't understand.
Healy's show wasn't always what it became. But the final form began in 1973, when the news hit that a couple of New York Yankees players had been swapping wives. That was a fastball down the middle for Healy, who interspersed his report of the news that night, and over the next several nights, with 18 clips of segments of the song from "Casablanca": "As Time Goes By."
Soon, the sound clips built up and became as familiar to his audience as their living room easy chair.
There was Charles Barkley, uttering his famous: "Bad team, man. Bad [bleeping] team."
There was Benoit Benjamin, the slow, fat and generally useless Clippers center: "I don't give a [bleep] about the fans."
There was Don King, getting befuddled in mid-bombast: "That is why we have a system of justice and Jewish-prudence."
There was Lawrence Welk, and his all-purpose: "A wun'erful, a wun'erful."
There was University of Miami football thug Jerome Brown, defending his team's rude behavior at a pre-bowl banquet: "Did the Japanese go and sit down and have dinner with Pearl Harbor before they bombed them?"
There was Victor Kiam, then the New England Patriots owner, trying to make amends after one of his players acted in a lewd manner in front of a female reporter: "She is a lovely lady and my apologies to her."
And there was the ever-present Howard Cosell, in full pomposity: "Who goofed? I've got to know."
Healy never shied from taking on the big guys. He called The Times sports section "The World Champion," and its sports editor "Journalist Bill." When the World Champion and Journalist Bill screwed up, which was often, there was no hiding: "Memo to Journalist Bill. [tickertape noise]. How about spelling words in headlines correctly? On Page 4, Karma should be with a K." (Who goofed? I've got to know).
Healy had news flooding in from everywhere. He had a million leakers, and it became a badge of honor to be one of his snoops. Sometimes, it almost seemed as if he were clairvoyant.
Once, a decision was made about a major firing in The Times' sports department, and Journalist Bill, who was going to do this Friday, told his wife about it Wednesday night. He told no one else. Thursday afternoon, Healy had it on the radio. Mrs. Journalist Bill has not been trusted since.
Many of Healy's scoops came from the World Champion's staff. The sports department bosses knew, made constant threats, and never stopped it.
"Your staff was like the Pentagon," Patrick Healy said recently. "They all leaked."
Such was the attraction of Jim Healy. He was crusty, insightful, cutting. And oh so much fun.
Ironically, the sports world that he covered so closely and held under such a strong microscope got him back in a proud moment. In the midst of the ceremony in 1991 in which his star was being put on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, word came that Magic Johnson had called a news conference, probably to announce that he had HIV. All the reporters, there to write and broadcast about Healy, left for Inglewood and the Forum.
For Healy, the timing was horrible.

user: What are the different career paths within the field of radiology?
response:
There are several different career paths within the field of radiology, including:

1. Radiologist: A medical doctor who specializes in the diagnosis and treatment of diseases and injuries using medical imaging technologies.

2. Radiologic Technologist: A healthcare worker who operates medical imaging equipment, such as X-ray machines and CT scanners, to produce diagnostic images.

3. Radiation Therapist: A healthcare worker who uses radiation to treat cancer and other diseases.

4. MRI Technologist: A healthcare worker who specializes in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which uses a magnetic field and radio waves to produce diagnostic images.

5. Nuclear Medicine Technologist: A healthcare worker who uses small amounts of radioactive materials to diagnose and treat diseases.

6. Sonographer: A healthcare worker who uses ultrasound technology to produce diagnostic images of the body's internal organs and tissues.

7. Medical Physicist: A healthcare worker who specializes in the use of radiation in medicine, including the development of new imaging technologies and the safe administration of radiation therapy.

8. Radiology Administrator: A healthcare professional who manages the operations and finances of radiology departments in hospitals, clinics, and other healthcare facilities.

response:
Introduction

Hydroponics is a soilless farming technique that is gaining popularity for sustainable food production. It involves the use of water, nutrients, and light to grow crops in controlled environments. With the increasing demand for food and the limited availability of arable land, hydroponics has the potential to revolutionize modern agriculture. However, there are still questions about its benefits and limitations in terms of sustainability, and research is needed to answer these questions. This proposal aims to explore the benefits and limitations of hydroponics for sustainable food production, propose specific research questions, and identify methods for data collection and analysis.

Literature Review

Hydroponics is a promising technique for sustainable food production. One of its major benefits is the ability to grow crops without the need for soil. This means that hydroponics is less reliant on arable land than traditional farming methods. It also reduces water usage by up to 90% compared to traditional methods (Tyson et al., 2019). Hydroponics can be used to grow crops in urban areas, where space is limited, and fresh produce is often scarce. Additionally, hydroponics can be used to grow crops in areas with poor soil quality, which saves time and resources that would have been used to improve the soil. With hydroponics, crops can be grown year-round in controlled environments that optimize growth and reduce crop losses from weather conditions and diseases.

One of the limitations of hydroponics is its reliance on technology, specifically electricity. Hydroponics require artificial lighting to provide the necessary light for photosynthesis, which increases electricity usage. Additionally, the initial investment in hydroponic technology can be costly, making it difficult for small-scale farmers to adopt this technology (Liu, 2015). A further limitation of hydroponics is that the system's reliance on chemical fertilizers, which have environmental implications such as water pollution, soil degradation, and health impacts for humans and animals consuming the crops.

Research Questions

1) What are the costs - benefit analysis of hydroponics farming in comparison to traditional farming? 
2) How does hydroponic technology contribute to sustainable food production? 
3) What are the environmental implications of hydroponics farming techniques? 
4) How can hydroponics technology be improved to maximize sustainable food production?

Hypothesis

Hydroponics technology has the potential to contribute significantly to sustainable food production, but its benefits and limitations require a thorough assessment. Addressing the environmental concerns associated with hydroponics technology is necessary for improving its sustainability.

Methodology

The proposed method of data collection is through primary and secondary data. The primary data will be collected through surveys of farmers practicing hydroponics to assess the costs and benefits of the technology versus traditional farming practices. The secondary data will involve reviewing past research and reports from credible sources to evaluate the environmental implications of hydroponics farming. Additionally, the data will be analyzed through statistical software such as Stata or SPSS to facilitate the presentation and interpretation of findings. 

Timeline 

Phase 1 (Week 1-2): Literature Review and Initial Research Planning 
Phase 2 (Week 2-4): Data Collection (surveys) 
Phase 3 (week 5-6): Data Analysis 
Phase 4 (week 7-8): Report Writing and Presentation 

Conclusion 

Hydroponics technology is a promising method for sustainable food production. Even though it has several benefits, there are limitations and environmental issues that need to be addressed before it can be widely adopted. Thus, research is vital in understanding these potential implications to improve hydroponics' sustainability. The study proposes the use of surveys, primary and secondary data to evaluate the costs and benefits of hydroponics technology as an alternative to traditional farming. This research aims to provide a broader perspective on the role of hydroponics in sustainable food production.

They were primarily pastoral nomads and established themselves as cattle herders and merchants, trading goods across the region. Eventually, they also became involved in Islamic scholarship and teaching, spreading their religion and language to new areas.

In the 19th century, the Fulani people came to power in several West African kingdoms through military conquest, such as the Sokoto Caliphate in Nigeria. This period saw the spread of Islamic law and culture throughout the region, which helped to unify the Fulani people and cement their place as a dominant ethnic group in West Africa.

Today, the Fulani people are found in many countries throughout West Africa, including Nigeria, Guinea, Mali, and Senegal, and are estimated to number over 40 million people.

Here is a piece of text: LUMA returns Friday, Sept. 1.
As the sky grows dark on Friday night, thousands of people are expected to fill the streets of downtown Binghamton for the third LUMA Projection Arts Festival.
On the corner of Court and Chenango streets, they'll tilt their heads up toward the dancing lights of a three-act drama played out upon the facade of a four-story gray building city residents, shopkeepers and patrons have walked by for nearly a century.
Its dual facades draw the eye to an apex where, by day, a towering grid of glass is bound by ionic columns, detailed ornamentation and varied depth.
But on this night, this building is one of LUMA's seven participating artists' chosen stage, where a mapped projection will unfurl an illuminated, vivid narrative of a young girl's imagination, and nearby, the production's creator will wait to hear a collective gasp.
"You will never see anything like this anywhere else," co-founder Nick Rubenstein said at a recent press conference. "The animations themselves will take the buildings and make them seem to come alive."
Since 2015, LUMA's combination of more than a dozen high-powered projectors and technology called 3D projection mapping has annually ushered more than 20,000 people into a two-block stretch of downtown Binghamton to watch artists transform the sides and faces of familiar buildings with animated visual displays.
It's the brainchild of co-founders Rubenstein, Joshua Bernard and Tice Lerner, and it started simply enough, an interest piqued by YouTube videos of powerful visual art displays around the world, followed by small-scale test runs fashioned from a white cardboard box and a borrowed projector and the evolution of an idea: to light up the city of Binghamton.
More common in Europe than in the United States at the time, LUMA creators have developed and grown the festival, now in its third year, through a combination of self-instruction and inspiration from other artists around the world, some whose work has appeared in the Netherlands, Spain and Hungary, but never in the United States.
On Friday, they join a list of artists performing in Binghamton.
"The thing I think we always stress is we want to be international," Lerner said at a recent press conference. "This is the year to do it."
Joining this year's LUMA lineup are Onionlab, a studio based in Barcelona, Spain, along with Maxin10sity, a studio based in Budapest, Hungary, who, in 2014, participated in one of the largest projections in the world, lighting up the 60,000-square-foot facade of the historic Palace of Parliament building in Bucharest.
"We're doing something I think four years ago you couldn't have imagined," Bernard said.
Others artists include Binghamton-based Lucem Picturae; Mark Zifchock, of Ithaca; Rama Karl, of California and Binghamton University's Jess Pelzar as well as Brooklyn-based Light Harvest.
"Not only is this an international festival with artists from all over the world," Lerner said, "but we've actually brought in some of the best in their field."
For internationally touring Light Harvest studio director Ryan Uzilevsky, LUMA provides an opportunity to tell a personal story and push this art form forward.
Audiences packed close on the city's roundabout at Court and Chenango streets on Friday will watch a grandfather inspire his granddaughter's imagination, said Uzilevsky, 35, of Brooklyn, and "see her mind unfold on the building."
It's the product of just over a month's worth of 16-hour days for the studio's artists, choreographers and actors, as the creative team digitally rebuilt the former Binghamton bank building "to the brick" in 3D and pre-recorded choreographed motion capture performances in New York City.
Inspired by Uzlivesky's grandfather, who died in 2016, the director — formerly a film director in California — said the piece draws on something his grandfather used to tell him: "We stand on the shoulders of the past."
Beyond what Uzlivesky calls "digital fireworks," he sees projection mapping as a platform for storytelling and hopes the projection will inspire young people "to be creative and think outside the box."
And just a few steps away from where this story will be told throughout the night, a studio from Budapest, Hungary, will recreate the story of another Binghamton landmark, the former home of the Carnegie Library on Exchange Street, in its projection called "Timeless Tales," and Onionlab, a studio hailing from Barcelona, Spain, will — with the help of 3D glasses — transform the dimensions of the Grand Royale Hotel around the corner.
"When you have a chance for artists to reimagine what architecture is, it's really exciting and gets the mind going," Uzlivesky said. "You get to do some really amazing things."
Held in conjunction with Binghamton's First Friday Art Walk, LUMA's citywide gallery has grown in the past three years and founders say it speaks to the city's revitalization.
"That's what LUMA is about," Bernard said. "It's about the arts, imagination. It's about what we all can be as a community."
As of Tuesday afternoon, $26,311 has been pledged to LUMA's Kickstarter fund by 447 contributors, exceeding the festival's goal of $25,000.
More buildings are involved in this year's event, as well as vendors and interactive experiences.

1. Cultural Exchange: The Crusaders were exposed to new cultures, religions, and ideas. They brought back with them spices, gold, and knowledge of medicine and architecture, leading to a cultural exchange that greatly impacted Europe.

2. Trade: The Crusades opened up new trade routes to the East, leading to a rise in trade and commerce. This led to the development of new industries such as banking, which helped fund future Crusades.

3. Military Technology: The Crusaders were exposed to new weapon technology, which helped them develop new military tactics and improve their weaponry, which further influenced Europe's military strategy.

4. Political Impact: The Crusades brought about significant changes in the political landscape of Europe. The Military Orders, such as the Templars, emerged as important political, economic, and social entities, while monarchs gained greater power by organizing and financing Crusades.

5. Religious Impact: The Crusades had a profound impact on religion. They led to the rise of religious fervor among Christians, while also contributing to the rise of religious anti-Semitism and the strengthening of the Muslim faith.

user: Discuss how to configure and manage a Elasticsearch cluster on Ubuntu.
response:
Elasticsearch is an open-source search and analytics engine that can be used to search, analyze, and store data. A cluster is a collection of nodes that work together as a single system. When Elasticsearch is deployed in a cluster, it provides improved fault tolerance, scalability, and performance. In this article, we will discuss how to configure and manage an Elasticsearch cluster on Ubuntu.

1. Installing Elasticsearch:

The first step in setting up an Elasticsearch cluster is to install it on all the nodes in the cluster. Here are the steps to install it on Ubuntu:

Step 1: Add the Elasticsearch repository:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install apt-transport-https
wget -qO - https://artifacts.elastic.co/GPG-KEY-elasticsearch | sudo apt-key add -
echo "deb https://artifacts.elastic.co/packages/7.x/apt stable main" | sudo tee -a /etc/apt/sources.list.d/elastic-7.x.list
sudo apt-get update

Step 2: Install Elasticsearch:

sudo apt-get install elasticsearch

2. Configuring Elasticsearch:

Once Elasticsearch is installed, the next step is to configure it. Here are the steps to configure Elasticsearch:

Step 1: Open the Elasticsearch configuration file:

sudo nano /etc/elasticsearch/elasticsearch.yml

Step 2: Configure the cluster name, node name, and network host:

cluster.name: mycluster
node.name: node1
network.host: 0.0.0.0

Step 3: Save and exit the configuration file.

3. Starting Elasticsearch:

After configuring Elasticsearch, the next step is to start it. Here are the steps to start Elasticsearch:

Step 1: Start Elasticsearch:

sudo systemctl start elasticsearch

Step 2: Check the status of Elasticsearch:

sudo systemctl status elasticsearch

4. Adding Nodes to the Elasticsearch Cluster:

To add nodes to the Elasticsearch cluster, follow these steps:

Step 1: Install Elasticsearch on the node.

Step 2: Open the Elasticsearch configuration file:

sudo nano /etc/elasticsearch/elasticsearch.yml

Step 3: Set the cluster name and node name:

cluster.name: mycluster
node.name: node2

Step 4: Set the network host:

network.host: 0.0.0.0

Step 5: Add the IP address of the other nodes in the cluster:

discovery.seed_hosts: ["node1_ip", "node2_ip", "node3_ip"]

Step 6: Save and exit the configuration file.

Step 7: Start the Elasticsearch service:

sudo systemctl start elasticsearch

5. Managing Elasticsearch Cluster:

To manage the Elasticsearch cluster, follow these steps:

Step 1: Check the status of all nodes in the cluster:

curl -X GET "http://localhost:9200/_cat/nodes?v"

Step 2: Check the status of the cluster:

curl -X GET "http://localhost:9200/_cluster/health?pretty"

Step 3: Add an index to Elasticsearch:

curl -X PUT "http://localhost:9200/my_index"

Step 4: Add a document to an index:

curl -X PUT "http://localhost:9200/my_index/_doc/1" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name": "John", "age": "30"}'

Step 5: Search for a document:

curl -X GET "http://localhost:9200/my_index/_search?q=name:John"

6. Conclusion:

In conclusion, Elasticsearch is a powerful search and analytics engine that can be used to search, analyze, and store data. By creating a cluster, you can improve fault tolerance, scalability, and performance. The steps above provide a guide on how to configure and manage an Elasticsearch cluster on Ubuntu.

Lately, his enthusiasm seems to be catching on. A growing army of “heirloom corn” fans, from celebrity chef Rick Bayless to food giants like ConAgra to a group of dogged Mexican scientists, are aiming to unlock the ancient ingredient to bring tortillas with better flavor to the high-end foodie market while boosting sustainable local economies.
Entrepreneurs see a huge profit to be made in higher-margin tortillas and chips sold at restaurants like Bayless’ Frontera Grill in Chicago and Enrique Olvera’s Cosme in New York, and mass marketed at higher-end retailers like Whole Foods Market Inc. It can also boost the incomes of the poor farmers in Mexico who have been cultivating traditional maize for millennia.
Several of the nearly 60 native varieties, or landraces, of this heirloom corn often grow alongside corn’s ancestor teocintle, a skimpy stalk with a few meager kernels that Mexican farmers transformed in a dizzying series of improvements over some 8,000 years.
Centuries later, their distant descendents see a bright future for the traditional grains if obstacles can be overcome.
The first is whether Mexican scientists can hammer out a first-ever fair trade certification for traditional corn farmers, similar to certifications for organic coffee or chocolate. Once an accord is reached, which is expected later this year, organizers say a civic association or panel of experts will provide the voluntary certification.
Another hurdle is the farmers themselves, many of whom are not fully versed about the value of their crops abroad, or even the specific variety of corn they tend. They also must ease their reliance on middle-men buyers known as coyotes who have long been their main sales channel and could be the losers if the crop’s value is enhanced.
If successful, exports of Mexico’s gourmet maize could start to reverse a flood of cheap U.S. Yellow corn imports that have pushed more than 1 million Mexican farmers off their fields since the enactment of the North American Free Trade Agreement in 1994.
“I live in GMO corn-country and it is the most tasteless corn in the world,” Bayless told Reuters, referring to the sprawling fields planted with genetically modified corn around his hometown Chicago, Illinois, America’s second biggest corn-producing state.
But the bolita variety of heirloom corn from Mexico’s southern Oaxaca state is different, he says.
The chef’s taste buds aren’t lying, the maize scientists behind the certification in Mexico say.
Commodity benchmark “Yellow 2” corn, a grain used mostly for animal feed, has little in common with Mexican corns that come in a kaleidoscope of colors and in some cases can be traced back for centuries to a specific mountain valley, says Flavio Aragon, one of the scientists behind the certification.
“The quality of Mexican corns is something else entirely,” he said.
Entrepreneurs putting big money on the line include Jorge Gaviria, chief executive of Los Angeles-based, privately-held Masienda, the first company to source the corn, whose ambition is to take on mass-produced tortillas with a tastier if pricier alternative.

U.S. Tortilla consumption is seen doubling to $30 billion by 2025, according to market research firm IndexBox.

The new landrace maize certification was expected to be ready late last year, but building consensus on the fine print has caused a delay.
Organizers say the certification will provide farmers with a document that details the specific variety they grow, the traditional farming methods they use. It would also restrict sales to surplus supply to prevent farmers from selling what they would normally set aside for their families and animals, forcing them to turn to more processed foods in their own diets.

Masienda, which sells directly to hundreds of restaurants, began buying Mexican heirloom corn three years ago. This season, its purchases will probably reach 2,000 tonnes, up five-fold since 2014, said Gaviria.
At the higher end, some heirloom varieties can already fetch around three times the price of conventional corns.

response:
The uncertainty principle is one of the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics that states that it is impossible to precisely determine certain pairs of physical properties of a particle, such as its position and momentum, at the same time. This principle is a manifestation of the wave-particle duality of quantum objects, where particles exhibit both wave-like and particle-like behaviors.

The role of observation in quantum mechanics is crucial since the act of measurement or observation can alter a particle's properties. In other words, the observer's interaction with the particle affects the outcome of the measurement, making it uncertain. This is known as the measurement problem and is a central aspect of quantum mechanics.

The uncertainty principle and the role of observation are closely related since the act of observation, or measurement, is limited by the uncertainty principle. The more precisely we measure one property of a particle, the less precisely we can measure the other, and this limits the accuracy of our observations.

Therefore, the uncertainty principle and the role of observation are intimately connected concepts in quantum mechanics that describe the fundamental limitations of our ability to measure the properties of particles.

Prior to the canal’s completion in 1914, ships had to travel around the southern tip of South America, adding thousands of miles and weeks to the journey. This increased transportation costs and limited trade between east and west.

After the canal’s construction, global trade patterns shifted dramatically. The canal reduced travel time and costs, leading to increased trade between the Atlantic and Pacific regions. Countries that were once isolated due to geographical barriers could now easily exchange goods and resources. As a result, the canal became a vital transportation hub that contributed to the growth of world trade and boosted global economic integration.

The construction of the canal also had a ripple effect on trade patterns far beyond the United States and Panama. Shipping routes between Asia and Europe, for example, were now shorter and more cost-effective, which led to the development of new trading partnerships and economic ties. The canal’s success also inspired the construction of similar shortcuts, such as the Suez Canal, which further facilitated trade between continents.

Overall, the construction of the Panama Canal has had a significant impact on global trade patterns and has played a crucial role in the development of the global economy.

Read the passage below and answer the question or follow the instruction: Can you summarize the history and current location of the Ragin' Cajun restaurant?

Passage: There are those of us who spent more than a few hours (and perhaps even days) sitting at the bar at the original Ragin’ Cajun on Pier Avenue in Hermosa Beach (now home to The Rockefeller), drinking a cold Dixie, eating some gumbalaya and contemplating the hot sauces that clustered like a miniature skyline on every table. There was Zydeco music in the air, the menus were hand-written on brown paper bags, and the waitresses were friendly as pie, and just as sweet. It was a really great place.
Then, after a contretemps with the landlord, it was sent into the Cajun version of a Babylonian Exile, with a Ragin’ Cajun food truck playing its wares on the streets of the South Bay. There was a relentless stream of rumors about the imminent reappearance of a brick-and-mortar Ragin’ Cajun — a restaurant that, like old Lazarus, would rise from the dead. The quirkiest (and most often heard) rumor had the Ragin’ Cajun being born again in the sprawling Plaza El Segundo on Sepulveda just north of Rosecrans, a well-polished setting that seemed antithetical to the eminent funk of the Ragin’ Cajun.
Perhaps it will yet rise in the center somewhere near the Veggie Grill. But right now, the Ragin’ Cajun lives again inside an affably shabby music venue called Suzy’s Bar & Grill in the comfortably rundown shopping center at the corner of Aviation and Prospect.
It’s a setting that would work in the Big Easy, where bending an elbow while running with the music and chewing on a po’ boy is a way of life. This isn’t quite the old Ragin’ Cajun — heck, nothing could be — but the crowd feels about right. This is not a room of financial advisers checking their iPhones. This is a space dedicated to folks who have been in the South Bay since the Ragin’ Cajun was the best place to eat for miles around. These are people who like to hang.
You can eat at the bar, you can eat at a number of four-tops, you can eat at some long tables where the crowd gets affable and there’s much talk about the relative merits of the hot sauces. These days, they come in bottles with the Ragin’ Cajun logo on them. These are house sauces, ranging from the expected to the, well, locally flavored. There’s Hot, Garlic and Pepper, along with Chipotle and Raspberry Chipotle. I suspect the first three would be recognizable on Bourbon Street; the last two might raise eyebrows.
There’s a somewhat simpler lunch menu at the Suzy’s edition of the Ragin’ Cajun that include grilled po’boys (chicken or a burger), fried po’boys (chicken, catfish, crawfish, oysters and shrimp — which is more like it!), combo plates of rice and beans and gumbalaya. Try the crawfish etoufee if you’re livin’ large or a lunch special like pork chops or sausage with rice and gravy, or a crawfish half and half.
At both lunch and dinner, there are cups and bowls of chicken and sausage gumbo, and the aforementioned gumbalaya (gumbo over jambalaya, an irresistible dish), along with salad with protein grilled, fried or blackened. This is a rare spot where you can lunch for about $5 (the cost of a cup of gumbo). That’s hard to beat.
But this is the cooking of N’Awlins and it deserves a certain amount of excess. Hush puppies are definitely called for. Maybe an appetizer order of fried catfish, crawfish, oysters or shrimp as well. And if it’s dinner time, along with the fried dinners, and the combo plates — all those red bean and rice concoctions with a gravy that’ll leave you thirsty for lots of beer — you can tuck into the blackened salmon, which does not blacken as well as Paul Prudhomme’s redfish, but it will do in a pinch.
The catfish etoufee (think a hyper spicy stew over rice) is a good thing; a taste of the French Quarter in Hermosa Beach. There’s a blackened ribeye as well, the most expensive item on the menu at $24.99 (many of the dishes cluster around $15). The menu tells us, “Blackened makes you say Ooh Wee!” The menu also tells us, “For no or very light seasoning, please let your server know!” This is a Cajun restaurant. I would be embarrassed.
This may not be the Ragin’ Cajun of memory, but it’s good to have it back. And the music reminds me of life on the street — even the air seems filled with the humid heat of a New Orleans night.

user: How do different types of seeds develop into plants and what factors contribute to their growth?
response:
Different types of seeds develop into plants through a process called germination. Germination is the process by which a seed sprouts and begins to grow into a plant. 

The factors that contribute to the growth of seeds and plants are water, nutrients, sunlight, and temperature. 

Water is essential for seed germination as it softens the seed coat and activates enzymes necessary for the plant to grow. Nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium are also important for plant growth and development. They provide the necessary building blocks for plant cells, proteins, and enzymes.

Sunlight is crucial for photosynthesis, which is the process by which plants convert light energy into chemical energy to fuel their growth. Without sunlight, plants cannot produce the energy they need to grow.

Temperature also plays a vital role in plant growth. Seeds and plants require a specific temperature range to germinate and grow. If the temperature is too high or too low, it can damage the plant's cells and slow down its growth.

Overall, the factors contributing to the growth of seeds and plants are interconnected, and any factor that is lacking can limit plant growth and development.

Generate according to: This traditional Italian chocolate dessert is gluten-free, rich and dense with chocolate and almonds and moisturized with olive oil. A decadent finale! Excellent served with espresso. Buon appetito!
Line a 9″ springform pan with parchment paper. Lightly oil the bottom.
Gently melt the chocolate and stir in the olive oil. Set aside.
Beat the sugar and 4 egg yolks until light and creamy.
Stir the ground almonds or almond flour into the sugar and egg mixture.
Gently stir in the melted chocolate and olive oil.
Beat the 4 egg whites with a pinch of cream of tartar until stiff peaks form.
Gradually fold the egg whites into the chocolate mixture. The mixture will not be light and airy but still rather dense.
Pour into prepared pan and bake for about 50 minutes. I usually start checking the cake at 40 minutes by inserting a toothpick in the center to see if the inside is still damp or beginning to form moist crumbs. This cake does have a fudgy inside so do not over bake it.
Let cool for half an hour and run a spatula around the edges to loosen the sides. Undo the sides of the pan and let cool. Cake can be kept for up to 5 days, wrapped in saran wrap in the refrigerator. It actually improves with flavor!
*I have made this cake using the full amount of mandarin oil and have also made it with half mandarin and half extra virgin olive oil. Feel free to improvise by using only extra virgin olive oil, eliminating the orange peel and perhaps stirring in a tsp. Of coffee power for a chocolate coffee flavor. This is porcini season in Italy. Restaurants eagerly feature this earthy mushroom delicacy in pastas, risottos, soups and more. I have hunted for them to no avail. If you are lucky enough to find or have a friend gift you these treasures, put them to good use in this recipe. Because I did not have fresh porcinis, I cleaned out my cupboard and used all the dried porcini I had collected over the years (probably saving them for some exotic recipe!) in this recipe. Dried porcinis can be found in most larger supermarkets and gourmet shops. My Porcini Soup is bold and rich, although it contains no cream. Feel free to add vegetable broth to dilute it if the flavor is too intense for you. I created this soup as a “primi” or starter to a meal because it is so light and delicate.
splash of Marsala wine – I used about 2 Tbls.
Place porcinis in a large bowl. Pour 5 Cups of hot water over the porcinis. Let rest for one hour or more. I soaked mine overnight but this is not necessary.
Heat olive oil in sauté pan and add the shallots. Cook under medium heat until soft and slightly caramelized.
Add the strained and slightly chopped porcinis.
Add the garlic and continue to cook slowly as to pull out the flavors of the aromatics. When the garlic is soft, pour the Marsala into the hot pan and cook for a minute.
Transfer the mixture into a saucepan. Strain the porcini liquid (to remove any dirt) into the sautéed mixture. Season with salt and white pepper. Do not under salt! Salt brings out the flavors of the mushrooms.
Pour into bowls and sprinkle with rosemary leaves. Feel free to improvise. Grate pecorino, parmesano, whatever sounds complimentary, over the top. I had some cooked faro so put it in the bottom of the bowl and poured the soup over it. Delicious and hearty! Drizzle with Frantoio Monet Olive Oil. Serve with a loaf of crusty bread.
response:
Porcini Soup Recipe:

Ingredients:
- 1 oz dried porcini mushrooms
- 5 cups hot water
- 1/4 cup olive oil
- 2 shallots, diced
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- Splash of Marsala wine (about 2 Tbls.)
- Salt and white pepper to taste
- Rosemary leaves, for garnish

Instructions:
1. In a large bowl, soak porcini mushrooms in hot water for one hour or more.
2. Heat olive oil in a sauté pan and cook shallots until soft and caramelized.
3. Add strained and chopped porcini mushrooms to the pan and cook slowly.
4. Add minced garlic and cook until soft.
5. Pour in the Marsala wine and cook for 1 minute.
6. Transfer the mixture to a saucepan and strain in the porcini liquid to remove dirt.
7. Season with salt and white pepper to taste.
8. Pour into bowls and garnish with rosemary leaves.

Serving Suggestions:
- Serve with a crusty bread for dipping.
- Add cooked farro or other grains to the soup for a heartier meal.
- Shave pecorino or parmesan cheese over the top for added flavor.
- Dilute with vegetable broth if the flavor is too intense.

Variations:
- Add cream to the soup for a richer flavor.
- Use fresh porcini mushrooms when in season.
- Serve over pasta for a main dish.
- Add other vegetables like carrots, celery, or onions for added texture.

Through the use of smart meters, customers can monitor their own energy usage and adjust their behavior accordingly to reduce costs and contribute to a more sustainable grid. To address these challenges, it will be important to ensure that adequate safeguards are in place to protect sensitive data and prevent unauthorized access to the grid.

user: Write a recipe for minestrone soup including ingredient measurements, cooking instructions, and any optional variations or substitutions. Please use clear and concise language that is easy to follow for novice cooks.
response:
Minestrone Soup Recipe

Ingredients:

- 1 tablespoon olive oil
- 1 onion, diced
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 carrots, diced
- 2 celery stalks, diced
- 1 can diced tomatoes (14 ounces)
- 1 can cannellini beans, drained and rinsed (14 ounces)
- 4 cups vegetable broth
- 1 zucchini, diced
- 1 cup small pasta (such as elbow or ditalini)
- 2 cups chopped kale or spinach
- Salt and pepper, to taste
- Freshly grated Parmesan cheese, for serving (optional)

Instructions:

1. Heat the olive oil in a large soup pot over medium heat.

2. Add the onion and garlic and cook for a couple of minutes until softened.

3. Add the carrots and celery and cook for another 5 minutes until slightly tender.

4. Stir in the diced tomatoes and cannellini beans.

5. Add the vegetable broth and bring everything to a boil.

6. Reduce heat to low and let the soup simmer for 20 minutes.

7. Add the zucchini and pasta to the soup and cook for another 10-12 minutes or until the pasta is tender.

8. Stir in the chopped kale or spinach and let it cook for 2-3 minutes or until wilted.

9. Season the soup with salt and pepper to taste.

10. Serve hot with freshly grated Parmesan cheese on top, if desired.

Optional Variations/Substitutions:

- Use chicken broth instead of vegetable broth for a non-vegetarian version.
- Add diced potatoes or sweet potatoes for extra heartiness.
- Use any type of pasta you have on hand or swap it out for quinoa or barley for added protein and texture.
- Add any extra vegetables you like (such as bell peppers, green beans, or peas) for more flavor and nutrition.

user: Create a Python program that utilizes the OpenCV library to read an image file in JPG format, applies the Canny edge detection algorithm with a threshold of 100 and saves the modified image as a PNG file under a new name. The program should also display both the original and modified images side by side using matplotlib.
response:
Import cv2
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# read image in JPG format
img = cv2.imread('image.jpg')

# apply Canny edge detection algorithm with threshold of 100
edges = cv2.Canny(img, 100, 200)

# save modified image as PNG file with new name
cv2.imwrite('modified_image.png', edges)

# display both original and modified images side by side
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2)
axs[0].imshow(cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB))
axs[0].set_title('Original Image')
axs[1].imshow(edges, cmap='gray')
axs[1].set_title('Modified Image (Canny Edge Detection)')
plt.show()

- 1/2 cup diced carrot
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 3 tablespoons butter
- 3 tablespoons all-purpose flour
- 3 cups fish stock or clam juice
- 2 cups milk
- 1 cup heavy cream
- 2 cups diced potatoes
- 2 teaspoons fresh thyme leaves
- Salt and pepper, to taste

1. Begin by selecting and preparing the seafood. Rinse the seafood under cold water to remove any grit or sand. Peel and devein the shrimp, and remove any shells or skin from the scallops and cod. Set aside.

2. In a large soup pot or Dutch oven, melt the butter over medium heat. Add the diced onions, celery, carrot, and garlic, and cook until softened, about 5 minutes.

3. Sprinkle the flour over the vegetables and stir until well combined, cooking for an additional 2-3 minutes.

4. Slowly add the fish stock or clam juice, whisking constantly to prevent any lumps from forming. Add the milk, heavy cream, diced potatoes, and thyme leaves. Increase the heat to medium-high and bring to a boil.

5. Reduce the heat to low and let the chowder simmer uncovered, stirring occasionally, until the potatoes are tender, about 20-25 minutes.

6. Add the mixed seafood to the pot and stir gently to combine. Let the chowder simmer for an additional 5-10 minutes, or until the seafood is cooked through and tender.

7. Season the chowder with salt and pepper to taste. Ladle into soup bowls and serve hot, garnished with fresh herbs or croutons if desired.

user: Develop a comprehensive research paper discussing the historical development and transformation of tapestry weaving throughout the ages, including its notable characteristics and changes in style, techniques, and materials used. Your paper should cover a range of topics, such as the early origins of tapestry weaving, notable artists and works, the emergence of different styles in different countries, the impact of the Industrial Revolution, modern technology and advancements, and the cultural significance of tapestry weaving in various societies. Be sure to cite relevant sources and provide a well-articulated conclusion that connects the historical evolution of tapestry weaving to its contemporary forms and applications.
response:
Introduction

Tapestry weaving is an ancient art form that has been in practice for centuries. The process involves weaving various fibers, such as wool, silk, and cotton, into intricate designs that depict scenes from history, mythology, and nature. Tapestry weaving has been used in many different cultures around the world, from Europe to Asia and Africa. This paper seeks to analyze the historical development and transformation of tapestry weaving throughout the ages, including notable characteristics and changes in style, techniques, and materials used.

Early Origins of Tapestry Weaving

The origins of tapestry weaving can be traced back to ancient Egypt, where textiles were woven with symbols and hieroglyphics. However, the art reached its zenith in the medieval period, particularly in the 14th and 15th centuries. The earliest surviving European tapestries date back to the early Middle Ages, and were mostly Gothic in style. These early tapestries, made in Germany and France, were used as curtains, bedspreads, and wall hangings.

Notable Artists and Works

Many notable artists have made a significant contribution to the development of tapestry weaving. One of the most famous is the Belgian artist Pieter Coecke van Aelst, who created some of the most remarkable tapestries in the 16th century. His work, The Triumph of Gaius, is regarded as one of the finest examples of Renaissance tapestry weaving, depicting a battle between the Romans and the Celts.

Another notable tapestry artist is Jean-Baptiste Oudry, who was responsible for weaving the tapestries for the Palace of Versailles in the 18th century. His work, The Hunt of the Unicorn, is considered one of the most significant tapestry creations of all time.

The Emergence of Different Styles in Different Countries

Different countries have their specific styles of tapestry weaving. For instance, French tapestries are known for their elaborate designs, while Flemish tapestries are known for their realistic details. Spanish tapestries are renowned for their landscaping, which depicted the landscapes of the time. Navajo tapestries from North America display geometric patterns in bright colors.

Impact of the Industrial Revolution

The Industrial Revolution had a significant impact on tapestry weaving. The invention of the jacquard loom in the early 19th century enabled the production of large-scale tapestries with intricate designs, which would have been impossible to achieve using traditional methods. These innovations in technology made tapestries cheaper to produce and more accessible to the middle class, who could own a piece of art that was previously the preserve of the aristocracy.

Modern Technology and Advancements

The introduction of modern technology has revolutionized tapestry weaving. Modern looms use computer technology to create intricate designs and color blends with incredible precision. Technical advancements have also enabled tapestries to be produced in different sizes, from small wall hangings to tapestries that cover entire walls.

Cultural Significance of Tapestry Weaving in Various Societies

Tapestry weaving has a rich cultural significance in various societies. For example, in the United States, Navajo textiles represent the history and cultural heritage of the Navajo people. In Europe, tapestries were used to depict the power and wealth of the nobility. In Africa, tapestries tell stories about the people, traditions and beliefs of different tribes. In modern times, tapestries are used for decorative purposes and as a way of preserving cultural heritage.

Conclusion

In conclusion, tapestry weaving has a fascinating history that has evolved over the centuries. The art form has undergone significant changes in style, techniques, and materials used. The early origins of tapestry weaving can be traced back to ancient Egypt. Notable artists such as Pieter Coecke van Aelst and Jean-Baptiste Oudry made significant contributions to the development of tapestry weaving during their time. Modern technology, including computer technology and technical advancements, has revolutionized tapestry weaving, enabling complex designs with incredible precision. Today, tapestry weaving continues to play a vital role in different cultures and societies across the world.

In contrast, solar energy can be deployed in a range of settings and does not require large-scale infrastructure.

response:
Ingredients:
- 4 red bell peppers
- 2 tablespoons of olive oil
- 1 onion, diced
- 4 cloves of garlic, minced
- 4 cups of vegetable broth
- 1 can of coconut milk
- 1 teaspoon of smoked paprika
- Salt and pepper to taste

Cooking equipment:
- Large baking sheet
- Blender or immersion blender
- Large pot
- Knife

Estimated cooking time:
- 45 minutes

Step-by-step recipe:

1. Preheat oven to 425°F (220°C).
2. Cut the red bell peppers in half and remove the seeds and stems.
3. Brush the peppers with olive oil and place them on a baking sheet, cut side down.
4. Roast the peppers for 20-25 minutes until the skin is slightly charred and the peppers are soft.
5. Remove the peppers from the oven and let them cool for 10-15 minutes.
6. Once cooled, peel off the skin from the peppers and discard.
7. In a large pot, heat 2 tablespoons of olive oil over medium heat.
8. Add the diced onion and minced garlic to the pot and cook until the onions become translucent.
9. Add the roasted red peppers, vegetable broth, coconut milk, smoked paprika, salt, and pepper to the pot and stir to combine.
10. Bring the soup to a boil, then reduce the heat and let it simmer for 20 minutes.
11. Use an immersion blender or transfer the soup to a blender to puree until smooth.
12. Serve the soup hot and garnish with fresh herbs or smoked paprika if desired.

Variations:
- Add roasted carrots or sweet potatoes for a sweeter soup.
- Swap out the smoked paprika for cumin or chili powder for a different flavor profile.
- Add a can of drained and rinsed chickpeas for protein and fiber.
- Top with a dollop of vegan sour cream or homemade croutons.

According to the story, a Bodhisattva - an enlightened being who has reached a high level of spiritual development - was walking through a forest when he came across a hungry tigress that was about to eat her cubs. The Bodhisattva saw that the tigress was so famished that she had no choice but to eat her own offspring.

The practice of self-sacrifice is important in Buddhism because it involves letting go of self-centeredness and the attachment to one's own physical and mental possessions. By giving away something that is valued, such as an arm, the Bodhisattva was able to detach himself from his own ego and demonstrate a profound sense of compassion for the tigress and her cubs.

Furthermore, the story also shows that detachment does not mean indifference - rather, the Bodhisattva was able to feel compassion for the tigress without being attached to his own body or material possessions. This detachment allowed him to act out of pure compassion, rather than out of personal gain or desire.

In conclusion, the story of the Bodhisattva and the Hungry Tigress is a powerful reminder of the importance of compassion, self-sacrifice, and detachment in Buddhism. Researchers design and test new materials for energy storage by following these steps:

1. Identifying the need: Researchers start by identifying the need for new materials that can provide better energy storage capabilities. They look for materials that can store more energy and release it efficiently.

2. Conceptualization: Once the need is identified, researchers brainstorm ideas for materials that can meet the need. They consider the chemical properties, molecular structure, and other characteristics of the materials.

3. Synthesis: Researchers then synthesize the materials using different methods such as chemical synthesis, electrochemical deposition, and sol-gel technique.

4. Fabrication: After synthesis, the materials need to be transformed into usable devices such as batteries or fuel cells. Researchers can use different fabrication methods such as printing, casting, or electrospinning.

5. Testing: The next step is to test the materials to evaluate their effectiveness. Researchers use various techniques like X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, Raman spectroscopy, and other analytical tools.

6. Optimization: Based on the results of testing, some materials may need further tweaking to enhance their energy storage capabilities. Researchers then optimize the materials by changing their structure or chemical composition.

7. Integration: After optimization, the materials are integrated into the final product such as a battery or fuel cell. This involves designing and constructing the device, testing it and evaluating its performance.

8. Scaling up: If the device performs well in the lab, the technology moves to a pilot plant or commercial production. The process of scaling up involves ensuring the device can function reliably in a large-scale production setting.

By following these steps, researchers can develop new materials for energy storage, with the potential to revolutionize the way we use energy.

Here are the key features of Baroque architecture:

1. Ornamentation: Baroque architecture heavily relies on decoration and ornamentation. It features ornate designs, intricate details, and strikingly beautiful sculptures.

2. Curvilinear Forms: Baroque architecture often features curved lines, skewed and dynamic shapes, undulating curves, and the use of asymmetrical designs.

3. Light and Shadow: One of the key features of Baroque architecture is how it uses light and shadow to create visual impact. The play of light and shadow is an important part of Baroque design, adding depth, dimension, and drama to buildings.

4. Grandiosity: Baroque architecture is characterized by its grandiose scale and majestic proportions. It often features large centralized areas, monumental entrances, and massive domes.

5. Illusionism: Baroque architects often used optical illusions to create the impression of greater size and depth in their buildings. These illusions were created through trompe l'oeil (trick of the eye) techniques.

6. Symmetry: Baroque architecture relies on the idea of symmetry to create a harmonious balance between different elements in a building. Symmetrical designs create a sense of order and stability, while asymmetrical designs create interest and movement.

7. Emphasis on Movement: Baroque architecture often emphasizes movement in its designs, through curving paths, staircases, and motion-oriented sculptures. This creates a sense of dynamism and energy within the building.

user: Write step-by-step instructions for creating a comprehensive family budget that includes all sources of income, monthly expenses, savings goals, and strategies for tracking and adjusting the budget as needed. Be sure to provide tips and examples for budgeting tools, such as online spreadsheets or budgeting apps, and address common challenges families may face when adhering to a budget, such as unexpected expenses or changes in income. Consider including a section on how to involve family members in the budgeting process and encourage communication and accountability.
response:
Step-by-Step Instructions for Creating a Comprehensive Family Budget

1. Determine all sources of income: Start by making a list of all the sources of income for your family. This may include salaries, bonuses, rental income, government benefits, and any other sources of income.

2. List your monthly expenses: Make a list of all the monthly expenses your family incurs, including rent or mortgage, food, utilities, insurance, car payments, gas, and any other regular expenses.

3. Set savings goals: Decide on your family's savings goals, such as creating an emergency fund, saving for a down payment on a house, or funding a college education.

4. Create a budget template: Use an online spreadsheet, a budgeting app or create a template in Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets.

5. Categorize expenses: Group similar expenses under categories. For example, group all utilities and bills under the utility category.

6. Assign budget amounts: Once you have all of your expenses categorized, assign a budget amount for each one. Assign reasonable amount, keeping some flexibility for unexpected expenses or emergencies.

7. Make adjustments: Once you have assigned a budget amount to each category, add up the total expenses, and compare that to your income. If expenses exceed income, re-evaluate each expense category and see where to cut back.

8. Track your spending: Record each expense throughout the month to keep track of how much you are spending on each category. This data can be used to spot any areas you're overspending or to see if you have enough money to make additional payments or savings contributions.

9. Review your budget regularly: Review your budget every month to see if you are sticking to your budget plan, to see if there are any unexpected expenses, or to adjust the budget in response to changes in income or expenses.

10. Encourage family involvement: Involve your family members in the budgeting process, so every member understands the family's financial goals and is accountable for contributing to the budget process. Create a family meeting to discuss the budget, any expense changes or upcoming events.

11. Use budgeting tools: Consider using budgeting apps like Mint or YNAB, which can help you track expenses and income in real-time, send alerts for bill payment deadlines or highlight categories where you're overspending.

12. Manage unexpected expenses: Even with a comprehensive budget, unexpected expenses will arise. Set aside some money each month for such expenses, so you are prepared for those cases.

By following these steps and utilizing budgeting tools, your family can create a comprehensive budget that will help you meet your financial goals and navigate the challenges of unexpected expenses and changes in income.

What are spheroid cultures, and what is their use in biological and ecotoxicological studies? How does the current study recommend the use of smaller spheroids to allow comparable oxygen concentrations to native tissues? Answer according to: A non-destructive technique which can measure the concentration and consumption of oxygen in 3D models of biological cells has been developed by Plymouth University in partnership with pharmaceutical company AstraZeneca.
Using Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) oximetry, scientists assessed the gradient of oxygen concentration within spheroids, 3D cell cultures typically used for testing the chemical toxicity within liver and tumour models.
It had previously been suggested that the centre of spheroid cultures becomes devoid of oxygen leading to cell death that may limit their use, but until now there has been no way of measuring the precise levels.
Work by PhD researcher Laura Langan and Senior Research Fellow Dr Nicholas Dodd demonstrated smaller spheroids with a diameter of less than 120 micrometres (µm), and containing fewer than 2,500 cells, lose less than 12 per cent of their oxygen concentration after one week decreasing to less than 50 per cent two weeks after their creation.
Overall, the study recommends the use of smaller spheroids to allow comparable oxygen concentrations to native tissues, with scientists believing the research provides further evidence of the appropriateness of these in vivo studies as a tool to elucidate fundamental biological processes in the spheroid systems and aid in the reduction of whole animal experiments.
Over the past three decades, the use of three dimensional cell culture has gained increased recognition as an important tool in biological research and pre-clinical trials over conventional organs and animal models.
Spheroids are one example of these, and are typically used to assess the chemical toxicity and evaluation of environmental samples in biological and ecotoxological studies.
Plymouth University has previously perfected the technique of coaxing cells from the liver of rainbow trout and then manipulating them to form a three-dimensional spheroid.
This ball of cells behaves much more like normal animal tissue than cells grown in traditional ways in the lab and so can give researchers a more accurate picture of how an animal’s body would respond to a chemical in the environment.
The current study is published in the PLOS ONE scientific journal, and the research team at Plymouth University has previously been awarded £600,000 by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC), the Natural Environmental Research Council (NERC) and AstraZeneca to work in this area.
The full paper – Direct Measurements of Oxygen Gradients in Spheroid Culture System using Electron Parametric Resonance Oxymetry by Langan, Dodd, Owen, Purcell, Jackson and Jha – is published in the PLOS ONE journal, doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0149492.
The School's strong and diverse research portfolio makes it a great place for research.
Non-invasive pre-natal testing, new targets for cancer treatment, understanding macrophages, combating sepsis and self-disseminating vaccines.

Ash Wednesday is an important day in Christian traditions, especially in the Roman Catholic, Anglican, and Eastern Orthodox churches. This day marks the beginning of Lent, a period of reflection, repentance, and spiritual preparation leading up to Easter Sunday, which commemorates the resurrection of Jesus Christ.

The purpose of Ash Wednesday is twofold. Firstly, it is a solemn reminder of human mortality and the need for repentance. During the Ash Wednesday service, worshippers receive a mark of ashes on their foreheads in the shape of a cross, which symbolize both death and resurrection, and reminds them of their own mortality and the need to repent and turn back to God.

Secondly, Ash Wednesday also marks the beginning of a 40-day period of fasting, penance, and spiritual reflection, in which Christians are called to give up something, such as a favorite food or activity, or take on a spiritual discipline, such as prayer or Bible study, to prepare themselves for the celebration of Easter.

Overall, Ash Wednesday is a day of solemn reflection and spiritual renewal, reminding Christians of their mortality, their need for repentance, and their call to a deeper relationship with God.

Can you summarize the author's experience of the holiday season, including their love of skiing, decked-out houses, and music? Answer according to: I do like the holiday season. Not everything about it, mind you, but many things. First, as an avid skier, I love the weather this time of the year—snow is my friend, and I don't mind the cold either (and no, I am not happy that we've not had much of either). Second, I love (most of) the decked-out houses in Baltimore neighborhoods. They range from tasteful white lights in trees to a myriad of biblical characters in various types of plastic, lit up in various colors, from Disney characters of the same make-up, to, of course, the pink flamingoes (that odd, almost quaint Baltimore tradition), all sitting peacefully one next to the other, on people's lawns.
I even like the music this time of the year. Being from Europe, a New Year doesn't start for me until I've watched the broadcast of Vienna Philharmonic's New Year's Concert, featuring many of the eternally elegant waltzes, coupled with the Lipizzaner horses, originally from the Slovenian Republic of my old country of Yugoslavia, dancing in sync with the music. Even the carols don't phase me, at least not in the first week or two of the season (though that period seems to come earlier every year, doesn't it, therefore lasting longer yet?).
This holiday season, I had an opportunity to hear an orchestra concert made up of talented students of A. Mario Loiederman Middle School in Montgomery County, that featured some of that holiday music. This is because I was given an opportunity to help them prepare (in a role of a conductor), during three visits, for a performance of Leroy Anderson's Sleigh Ride, that culminated in that concert.
Most of these kids are learning their instruments without the benefit of private lessons. A lot of them haven't even had a chance to learn how to properly hold their instrument or decipher some of the very basic note reading, let alone learn ways to mold a phrase or deliver dynamics the composer is requiring. But they make up for it in enthusiasm and youthful energy.
This is where their music teachers, in this case Ian Stuart and Liz Jankowski-Carson, enter into the equation. I have always considered the grossly underpaid music teachers in elementary and middle schools in this country to be the real heroes of our music industry. Day in and day out, they deal with kids who are playing on instruments that are sometimes missing proper reeds, strings, or are impossible to tune, kids that are sometimes lacking the capacity to be quiet, listen and concentrate at the high level that is required for any progress to occur in an ensemble rehearsal. Sometimes they have to politely ask and plead, other times turn into task masters the likes of boot camp officers, in order to get anything done. To say that rehearsing a 3 minute arrangement of the Sleigh Ride with these kids for a couple of hours is a challenge is a gross understatement.
Yet they (the teachers) perform small miracles every day. It was intriguing to see Mr. Stewart get them pepped up, yet keep them disciplined and quiet as they were preparing for their performance.
I listened to several jazz, pop and rock music-influenced holiday tunes backstage while waiting to conduct them in the Anderson, and observed the same types of communication that are necessary to pull off a performance anywhere, on any stage. Smiles and stern looks rained on them from their conductors'/teachers' faces, other sections were listened to for cues, eyes darted alternately from the music to conductor's baton, it all was there. Not all the notes were there, of course, and not every nuance came through, but it was all done with a great amount of energy and pride.
The same was true with the Sleigh Ride. I saw the whites of their eyes in crucial spots in the percussion, smiles from cellos in their fun counter-melodies, heard strong rhythm from brass and woodwinds and great dynamics from the violins and violas. The crowd, made up of very enthusiastic parents, teachers, and fellow students, exploded in appreciative applause. A great reward for the many hours of work the kids and their teachers put into the challenging program.
So, even though it may seem like a distant memory now, I remember with fondness the good time we all had in the last holiday season, and look forward to returning to the Loiederman School for more coachings and rehearsals in the spring, when this winter also becomes a just a distant memory.
During the holiday season there are a lot of pleasant and positive emotions around because all people enjoy their holidays and enjoy their time.

Introduction

The field of science and scientific research is constantly evolving. The viability of a scientific model or theory is determined by its consistency with existing empirical evidence, its ability to make testable predictions, and its potential for guiding future research. In this essay, I will argue in support of the scientific model that climate change is primarily caused by human activity.

Consistency with Existing Empirical Evidence

One of the strongest pieces of evidence supporting the idea that climate change is caused by human activity is the consistent increase in temperatures over the last century. According to NASA, the average temperature of the Earth's surface has increased by approximately 1°C since the late 19th century, with the majority of the warming occurring in the last few decades. This increase in temperature is consistent with the build-up of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, which has been caused primarily by human activity such as factory emissions, transportation, and deforestation.

Additionally, repeated analysis of ice core samples from the Arctic and Antarctic has shown an undeniable correlation between elevated carbon dioxide levels and increased temperatures. Moreover, the Arctic sea ice has been declining at a rate of 12.8% per decade since records began, including a record minimum in 2020, which is attributable to human-induced warming.

Testable Predictions

The theory that climate change is driven primarily by human activity made several testable predictions. For instance, it predicted that as CO2 concentrations increased, temperatures would also increase. This has been observed consistently, as temperatures have increased alongside greenhouse gas concentrations.

Climate models also predicted that warming would be most pronounced in high latitude regions of the planet, such as the Arctic Circle, due to the decrease in ice coverage, causing decreased reflection of sunlight back to space, which amplifies the warming. This prediction is now evident in the Arctic's sharp increase in temperature compared to warming in other areas of the planet.

Guiding Future Research

The hypothesis that climate change is primarily caused by human activity guides future research. For instance, scientists develop new models that can predict how CO2 and other greenhouse gases will interact with the atmosphere in the coming years with different emission scenarios. Researchers have investigated whether widespread adoption of renewable energy would curb greenhouse emissions and their associated warming.

Counterarguments and Alternative Hypotheses

Some argue that natural climatic variability, such as solar radiation fluctuations, volcanic activity, and changes in ocean circulation, could be the primary cause of climate change. Other more far-fetched "alternative" explanations include changes in Earth's axis tilt, cosmic ray fluxes from explosions of stars, etc. Nonetheless, studies have shown the influence such natural variations have relatively insignificant when compared to the significant increases in energy and heat-trapping gas emissions from human activities.

Implications of Accepting or Rejecting the Model or Theory

The acceptance of the scientific model that climate change is primarily caused by human activity warrants action towards reducing greenhouse gas emissions, promoting renewable energy adoption, and incorporating financial instruments and policies to incentivize individuals and corporations to limit their carbon footprint.

The rejection of the models that climate change is primarily caused by human activity would signify that society should continue to emit greenhouse gases into the atmosphere unmitigated. This would endanger numerous ecosystems and has already led to severe weather conditions associated with unmitigated warming such as droughts, wildfires, increased frequency of hurricanes, and rising sea levels.

Conclusion

The overwhelming evidence supporting the hypothesis that climate change is primarily caused by humans makes it a scientifically viable model. Its consistency with existing empirical evidence, ability to make testable predictions, and potential for guiding future research make it a vital call to action. Addressing climate change requires policymakers to consider scientific facts and observations as the primary guide for crafting policies that avert dangerous conditions for future generations.

user: Write a Lisp program using recursion that takes in a list of integers and finds the minimum and maximum values. The program should output the minimum and maximum values, as well as the number of iterations it took to find them. Your program should not use any built-in functions that directly find the minimum or maximum values, but must manually traverse the list.
response:
Here is one possible implementation in Lisp:

```lisp
(defun find-min-max (lst)
  (labels ((helper (lst min max cnt)
             (cond ((null lst) (values min max cnt))
                   ((< (car lst) min)
                    (helper (cdr lst) (car lst) max (1+ cnt)))
                   ((> (car lst) max)
                    (helper (cdr lst) min (car lst) (1+ cnt)))
                   (t (helper (cdr lst) min max (1+ cnt))))))
    (helper (cdr lst) (car lst) (car lst) 1)))

;; example usage:
(find-min-max '(3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 5 3 5 8))
;; => returns multiple values:
;;      1 ; minimum value
;;      9 ; maximum value
;;      12 ; number of iterations
```

The `find-min-max` function takes in a list of integers `lst` and calls a helper function `helper` to recursively traverse the list and keep track of the minimum and maximum values seen so far (`min` and `max`) as well as the number of iterations (`cnt`). The function uses the `defun` and `labels` special forms to define the helper function within the scope of `find-min-max`.

The `helper` function takes in the same parameters as `find-min-max` as well as the current element `car lst` of the list being traversed. It checks if the current element is lower or higher than the current minimum or maximum values respectively, and updates those values accordingly. It then calls itself recursively with the rest of the list `cdr lst` and the updated values, and increments the counter `cnt` by 1. If the list is empty, the function returns the minimum and maximum values along with the final value of the counter using the `values` function.

The example usage shows how to call the function on a sample list of integers and retrieve the minimum and maximum values along with the number of iterations. Note that since `values` returns multiple values, we can separate them with semicolons in the comments for clarity.

How to Make a Handmade Candle

Candles are a great way to add warmth, ambiance, and fragrance to any setting. While store-bought candles can be expensive, making your own candles at home is affordable and easy. In this step-by-step tutorial, we'll show you how to make a handmade candle using materials easily found at home, such as beeswax, soy wax, or paraffin wax.

Materials Needed:

- Wax (beeswax, soy wax, or paraffin wax)
- Wick
- Container (a jar or tin)
- Fragrance oil or essential oil (optional)
- Wax dye or crayons (optional)
- Double boiler or pot and metal bowl
- Thermometer
- Stirring utensil
- Scissors
- Tape

Step 1: Choose your Wax

The type of wax you choose will determine the texture, color, and burn time of your candle. Beeswax is a natural and eco-friendly option, but it is more expensive than soy or paraffin wax. Soy wax is made from soybeans and is vegan and renewable. Paraffin wax is the most affordable choice and provides a smooth and shiny finish. Choose the wax that suits your preference and budget.

Step 2: Select your Wick

The size and type of wick you choose will depend on the diameter of your container and the type of wax you are using. Check the label of your wax or use a wick size chart to determine the appropriate wick size. If you are using a thick container, you may need to use multiple wicks. Be sure to use cotton or wooden wicks, as they are the safest and most eco-friendly options.

Step 3: Choose your Container and Fragrance

Select a container that is heat-resistant and appropriate for the size of your candle. A wide-mouth jar or a tin can are great options. If you want your candle to be scented, choose a fragrance oil or essential oil that you like. Essential oils are natural and last longer, but fragrance oils offer a wider range of scents.

Step 4: Melt the Wax

Using a double boiler or a pot and a metal bowl, melt the wax over low heat. Do not leave the wax unattended, and stir it frequently to avoid overheating. Use a thermometer to check the temperature of the wax. Soy wax should be heated to 130-140°F, beeswax to 145°F, and paraffin wax to 175°F.

Step 5: Add Color and Fragrance (optional)

If you want to add color to your candle, use dye chips or crayons to achieve the desired hue. Add the dye slowly, stirring constantly until it dissolves. If you want your candle to be scented, add the fragrance oil or essential oil to the melted wax, stirring well.

Step 6: Prepare the Wick and Container

Center the wick in the container and secure it in place with a bit of tape. Cut the excess wick, leaving ⅛-¼ inch above the wax surface. Hold the wick upright with a wick holder or a pencil.

Step 7: Pour the Wax

Slowly pour the melted wax into the container, being careful not to pour it too quickly, which can cause air bubbles. Leave a small amount of wax in the pot in case you need to top off your candle later. Let the candle cool and harden completely, which may take a few hours.

Step 8: Trim the Wick and Burn Safely

Trim the wick to ¼ inch above the wax surface. Burn the candle on a heat-resistant surface away from flammable materials, and never leave it unattended. To avoid tunneling, make sure to burn the candle for several hours, allowing the melted wax to reach the edges. If frosting occurs, it is a natural occurrence and does not affect the candle's performance.

Conclusion

Making your own candles is a fun and rewarding activity that can save you money and allow you to customize the scent and appearance of your candles. With these simple steps, you can create beautiful and fragrant candles using materials easily found at home. Always burn candles safely and follow these tips to ensure optimal performance and longevity.
